questions.question: Which boundary keeps normal playback bytes away from application servers?
options: The player sends every segment through the catalog service
The playback service authorizes once, then the player fetches manifests and segments from CDN hostnames
The analytics pipeline proxies all media
The transcoder streams directly to every viewer
questions.explanation: The control plane authorizes and selects a publication; the media plane delivers immutable bytes through the CDN.

questions.question: What is the safest publication invariant?
options: A manifest may reference segments while workers are still writing them
Popular videos may skip integrity checks
A published manifest references only complete, authorized, immutable segments from one validated version
Every rendition must use the newest codec
questions.explanation: Completeness, authorization, immutability, and one coherent version prevent partial or mixed playback.

questions.question: Two million viewers average 3.5 Mbps. Approximately how much aggregate edge bandwidth is required?
options: 0.56 Tbps
3.5 Tbps
7 Tbps
70 Tbps
questions.explanation: 2,000,000 multiplied by 3.5 Mbps is 7,000,000 Mbps, or about 7 Tbps.

questions.question: Why track byte cache hit rate in addition to request hit rate?
options: Large high-bitrate misses can dominate origin bandwidth even when many small requests hit
Request hit rate already includes transcoding cost
Byte hit rate proves authorization correctness
Only manifests use request hit rate
questions.explanation: Origin exposure depends on missed bytes, not just the number of missed requests.

questions.question: What should happen when many edges miss the same newly popular segment?
options: Every viewer retries object storage independently
Disable caching
Coalesce fills at an origin shield and cap upstream concurrency
Publish a mutable segment URL
questions.explanation: Request coalescing turns many simultaneous misses into a bounded number of upstream fills.

questions.question: Why align segment boundaries across renditions?
options: It lets the player switch quality without timeline gaps
It makes authorization unnecessary
It guarantees every codec has the same file size
It removes the need for manifests
questions.explanation: Aligned timelines allow adaptive quality switches at common media boundaries.

questions.question: Which data needs the strongest transition semantics?
options: Approximate view counters
Sampled player telemetry
The active publication pointer and video visibility
Daily popularity aggregates
questions.explanation: The active version and visibility decide which bytes are safe and authorized to serve.

questions.question: What is the most defensible degraded mode during constrained delivery capacity?
options: Keep requesting the highest rendition until playback stalls
Serve a lower compatible rendition and use bounded failover while protecting the origin
Skip manifest validation
Block all existing sessions when analytics is unavailable
questions.explanation: Lowering byte demand and using bounded failover protects playback continuity and shared infrastructure.
